items.passage: Who brings a ferry token to a wedding? Mele wondered, watching Leilani turn the brass coin across her knuckles while the band tuned up in the crowded Auckland hall. Years ago, on stormy mornings, Leilani's father had pressed one into each passenger's hand at the gangway and collected it again on the far shore; a token, he liked to say, was only ever surrendered by someone who had arrived. Tonight Mele was waiting on a message from the hospital, where her brother had been in surgery since noon. During the speeches, Leilani set the coin in Mele's palm without a word. Mele held it through the toasts and the first dance, rubbing its worn rim whenever her phone stayed dark. When the screen finally lit, she did not read it at once; she closed her fingers around the brass first, then looked. Across the room, guests clapped as the couple cut a cake iced with tiny white sails.
items.question: In the text, the ferry token most likely represents
options: the fare that Mele still owes for the many crossings she once made on the ferry.
Leilani's longing for the harbor life she left behind when her father retired.
the newly married couple's hope for a long and steady voyage through marriage.
an assurance of safe passage that Mele holds onto as she waits for word.

items.passage: Cut grass and wet chalk are what I remember of the Taipei field the week after I missed the penalty in front of the whole stadium. Coach Yuxuan benched me without a word of explanation. Each evening at dusk she handed me a flat ball from the shed and a hand pump, and I knelt by the sideline while the others ran drills. I pumped carelessly at first, and by morning the ball sagged again, soft as my own legs had felt at the spot. Midweek I began to check the valve, press the seams, and test the bounce against my palm before returning it. Yuxuan said nothing about this; she only began handing me the ball a little earlier each night. On the seventh evening she bounced it once, hard, on the grass and nodded toward the goal. Overhead, the floodlights buzzed awake one bank at a time, and moths gathered in the glare.

options: the routine chores that Yuxuan assigns to teach Ruoxi obedience to team rules.
the growing trust between Yuxuan and Ruoxi as they work side by side each night.

Ruoxi's self-assurance, which her failure deflated and she slowly rebuilds.

items.passage: Jeju Island had only one bus stop on that stretch of the mountain road, a tin shelter where Minjun waited after school. On Monday she had told a single classmate, in a whisper behind the gym, that her father was not coming back from Busan. By Wednesday the fishmonger had stopped charging her for squid, and the nurse at the clinic had squeezed her shoulder for no reason she could name. On Friday Eamon, who had fished beside her father for twenty years, sat down in the shelter and said her aunt had heard. The news had grown legs of its own, he added, and had not asked her permission to use them. He offered her a tangerine and said her aunt was not angry, only sorry to have learned it from a neighbor. Minjun peeled the fruit slowly. Mist slid over the ridge, and the bus appeared, its headlights soft in the gray.
items.question: As used in the text, the phrase “grown legs of its own” most nearly suggests that the news
options: had been exaggerated by each neighbor until it no longer matched the truth.
had traveled slowly because few people in the village cared to repeat it.
had moved from one person to another in ways Minjun could not direct.
had been carried by Eamon himself on his walk down to her aunt's house.

items.passage: Kyoto's eastern hills were slick with rain when the funicular stalled halfway up, and the attendant led its two passengers onto a terrace café to wait. Takeshi took the table farthest from Kenji, nodded once, and opened a newspaper he did not read. Kenji ordered tea and remarked on the weather to no one in particular. For twenty minutes their only exchange concerned the sugar bowl. Then the owner set down a dish of pickled plums, and Kenji, tasting one, said quietly that his late grandmother had made them saltier, with a shiso leaf folded inside each. Takeshi lowered the paper. His mother had done the same, he said, and had never written the method down. Kenji pulled his chair across the terrace. Soon a napkin between them was crowded with figures, half of them crossed out, and each man was insisting, between bursts of laughter, that the leaves must dry a day longer or a day less. Below the railing, rain kept dripping from the maples into the moss.
items.question: Which choice best describes the shift in tone that occurs in the text?
options: From reserved distance to lively, shared enthusiasm
From awkward silence to wistful, private sorrow
From mild irritation to grudging, polite acceptance
From polite curiosity to tense, open rivalry

items.passage: I sold the lamp. That was how I, Astrid, began my confession to Nargis when she found me at the open-air market in Tromso one Saturday in 1911. She had come north to survey the coast and had lodged two months at my lighthouse. On her first night she admired my father's brass lamp, calling it the only warm thing in the tower. Each dawn after that, I watched her leave for the fjord in a coat cut for a southern autumn, and each evening she stamped her feet a long while by the stove. Once she joked that her boots let in more sea than they kept out. While she was measuring inlets, I carried the lamp down the hill. With the coins I bought heavy wool and paid the cobbler's stall to resole her boots. Around us fish sellers shouted prices, and gulls quarreled over a dropped herring.

options: She feels guilty that her father's lamp has gone unused since his death.
She hopes the gifts will win Nargis's thanks and persuade her to stay longer.
She needs coins because the lighthouse has gone without its winter supplies.
She wants to remedy hardships of Nargis's that she has quietly observed.

items.passage: Cairo had stayed behind on the far side of the canal, and the farmhouse I had rented seemed to belong to no city at all. On my first morning, Thida showed me the lemon tree by the well, a graft she had bound to a wild root years before. A pale ring still marked where the two barks had met and, for a season, refused to agree. When she asked how long I meant to stay, I said I had not unpacked enough to know. Thida only tightened the old twine around a new cutting and said grafts take best when no one hovers over them. I hovered anyway. Each evening before supper I walked to the tree and pressed my thumb to the ring, as if checking a pulse, and afterward I unpacked one more box. By the month's end a single green shoot had pushed out just above the scar. In the kitchen the kettle whistled, and the shutters knocked against the frame in the wind.
items.question: In the text, the grafted lemon tree most likely symbolizes
options: Thida's long devotion to the farmhouse garden and its earlier tenants
the narrator's lingering sorrow over the city life she has left behind
the narrator's slow attempt to make a home in an unfamiliar place
the uneasy partnership growing between the narrator and Thida

items.passage: Ramses Station, in the autumn of 1987, kept a narrow cafe beside platform four where students waited out delays over sweet tea. Every Thursday Yasmin came there to pay Karim, her younger brother's tutor, from an envelope she had counted twice at home. He always handed back the last coin, claiming with a grin that inflation had not yet reached algebra. Yasmin did not argue. On her way out, she dropped the coin into a chipped glass jar by the register, where the waiter gathered change for the boy who swept the platforms. Some weeks later Karim, finishing his tea, began dropping his own spare piastres in after hers. By spring the jar was nearly full, its coins dulled from handling, and the sweeping boy wore a pair of new shoes. When the trains at last ran on time again, the cafe rearranged its tables, and the jar moved to a shelf above the sugar.
items.question: In the text, the glass jar most likely symbolizes
options: a kindness that Yasmin and Karim build together without ever naming it
the savings Yasmin sets aside in case her brother's lessons cost more
Karim's quiet pride, which keeps him from accepting full payment
the cafe's habit of collecting coins to survive the station's delays

items.passage: Sunethra kept the keeper's lodge at the reservoir above Lisbon in the drought year of 1868, and I was the hiker who stumbled out of her pines after two nights astray. She fed me, dried my boots by her stove, and asked little except whether anyone was waiting for me in the city. On the third morning she walked me to the end of the dock, where a lantern hung on a post, and lit it although the sun was already high. A handshake would do, I told her, laughing. She said her lantern did not care what I thought it should do. From the ridge, an hour later, I looked back and found the small flame still burning above the water, long after the lodge had vanished behind the trees. I walked the rest of the way more slowly than I needed to. Years afterward, when I told the story, I could never recall whether I had waved.
items.question: In the text, the lantern on the dock most likely represents
options: a warning Sunethra gives travelers about the dangers of the hills
Sunethra's concern for Joaquim, extended beyond their parting
Sunethra's loneliness at the lodge once her visitors have gone
an old custom that Joaquim finds amusing and soon forgets

items.passage: When Camila found the photograph in my old sea chest, she carried it out to the orchard where I sat among the dead mango trees. In the picture I was twenty, grinning on a freighter's deck, my arm around a man I had not mentioned in forty years. Dario, she asked, who is he? I told her the trees had stopped bearing the summer I came home. She did not let me change the subject; she set the photograph on my knee and waited. The memory lay in my chest like an anchor fouled on the seabed, and every attempt I made to raise it only drew the line tight. Then, with her still beside me, saying nothing, I began to tell her about the storm off Veracruz. Camila listened, peeling a dry branch into strips, while the wind moved through the bare limbs overhead.
items.question: As used in the text, the phrase “like an anchor fouled on the seabed” most nearly suggests that the memory
options: had kept the narrator steady through his many lonely years ashore.
had sunk so deep that the narrator could no longer recall its details.
was lodged so firmly that the narrator could not bring it up by himself.
threatened to drag the narrator back toward the dangers of his years at sea.

items.passage:
When the mourners left the hall in Chengdu,
Jianguo and I walked to the salt-water baths
our grandfather had built in the year of floods.
Eleni, he asked, you passed your examinations?
I nodded, and the lie went under
like a stone into the brine,
where nothing sinks quite all the way.

We sat on the tiled edge, feet in the green water.
He spoke of the ledger he had kept for the old man,
of figures he had copied twice.
All the while I kept glancing down,
as if something pale might rise
and turn its face toward him.

Above the pool the paper lanterns swung,
and someone in the courtyard swept the ash.
items.question: As used in the text, the phrase “where nothing sinks quite all the way” most nearly suggests that the speaker's lie
options: stays near the surface of her mind and cannot be fully put away
dissolves slowly until it no longer troubles the speaker at all
has already been guessed by Jianguo, who hides a failure of his own
grows heavier and heavier the longer she keeps it from her cousin

items.passage: What does a town do when its two oldest customs both claim the same evening? In the Riga suburb where I grew up, the answer was worked out in 1991 at the back of Vesna's shoe repair stall, because she was mayor and the stall had the only table long enough. Pavel, the town's only doctor, wanted the midsummer supper to follow his family's Orthodox fast; Vesna's neighbors wanted the old Latvian songs and the cheese with caraway. For an hour they argued over awls and heel nails. Then Pavel picked up a needle from the bench and said the whole matter was a question of stitching. Two leathers of different grain, he explained, could still be sewn into a single sole if the thread was patient. By midnight the menu listed the fasting dishes and the caraway cheese on facing halves of one card. Vesna's stall sells phones now, though the long table still stands in the back.
items.question: As used in the text, the phrase “sewn into a single sole” most nearly suggests
options: patching over an argument so that no one would raise it again
uniting two distinct customs in a single shared supper
replacing both old customs with a new tradition of the town's own
settling the dispute by letting one custom absorb the other

items.passage: Tell me about the trading post first, Aponi said, before I had even set down my bundle. So I told her. We stood on the stone bridge below the mesa in the spring of 1879, a year after my family had gone east, and I described my father's ledgers and the schoolmaster's squeaking boots until she laughed. Once, when we were nine, her brother had dared us both to walk the parapet; the summer before I left, the flood had taken him from beneath these same arches. Neither of us mentioned him. For two days we grazed our talk around the edges of one pasture, wandering wide to horses, to weather, to the price of wool. Whenever the water grew loud below us, she would point out a hawk, and I would look where she pointed, though I saw no hawk. On the third evening she pressed a smooth river stone into my palm without explaining it, and I carried it east in my coat. Shadows of the arches lay long across the dry wash, and somewhere up the slope a dog was bringing the sheep down.
items.question: As used in the text, the phrase “grazed our talk around the edges of one pasture” most nearly suggests
options: a habit of filling the awkwardness of a long separation with small talk.
Omar's quiet effort to shield Aponi from news she had not yet heard.
a shared, deliberate steering of conversation away from one painful subject.
a lingering dispute over the grazing land each family claimed near the bridge.

items.passage: When Paloma handed me the ring of keys that morning, she bowed as if presenting a crown, and I laughed so hard I nearly dropped them. The salt-water pool behind the Dayton rec center had been hers for thirty summers; I was nineteen, her apprentice, and the aquatic park across town had just offered me twice her wage. I mentioned it while we skimmed leaves. Paloma asked whether they would give me a whistle with my name engraved on it, and maybe a manager younger than my sneakers. We traded jabs down the length of the deep end. Then, testing the water, she held the vial up to the light longer than she needed to. Her father's crew had poured these walls, she said. Every child on Fifth Street had learned to float in the shallow end, me included, and the drain still stuck each November in a way no manual explained. She did not ask me to stay. She only showed me, slowly, where to kick the grate. I set down the net. Across the water, light lay flat on the tiles, and a dragonfly kept touching the surface and lifting away.
items.question: Which choice best describes the shift in tone that occurs in the text?
options: It moves from affectionate joking to wounded reproach as Paloma faults the narrator for leaving.
It moves from nervous uncertainty to firm resolve as the narrator commits to the new job.
It moves from brisk instruction to lighthearted teasing as Paloma eases the morning's tension.
It moves from lighthearted teasing to quiet earnestness as Paloma passes on what she knows.

items.passage: Hasan counted chairs. At every wedding we staffed in Thessaloniki that summer of 1872, he circled the hall twice before the guests came, tapping each chair back like a priest blessing pews, and I, newly hired, learned to time my yawns to the movement of his lips. That evening the count collapsed within minutes: cousins perched on window ledges, the musicians spilled down the stairs, and an aunt sat squarely on his tally board. I braced for thunder. None came. Hasan stood among the dancers with his hands loose at his sides, watching a boy asleep across two laps. Much later, as we folded linens, he mentioned that his father had once lost a post over a single guest left standing, and that he had counted chairs every night since, though no one had ever asked him to. Then he set his tally slate on my stack of napkins. Keep it or break it, Sadia, he said, and went to help the cooks. Out on the street, a cart wheel ground slowly over the wet stones.
items.question: Which choice best describes the shift in tone that occurs in the text?
options: It shifts from wry amusement at Hasan's ritual to a gentle, reflective sympathy.
It shifts from wry amusement at Hasan's ritual to nervous dread of his temper.
It shifts from quiet boredom with the work to exuberant joy at the crowded feast.
It shifts from mocking impatience with Hasan to admiration for his strict precision.

items.passage: Four objects lived in Jomo's back room: a treadle machine, a headless dressmaker's dummy, a radio that caught one station, and the runner-up plate from the 1979 district chess final, which he had lost to me when I was twelve. For ten years I had let people call me brilliant for beating a grown man. That afternoon I sat on his cutting table while he hemmed a pair of trousers, and I asked, idly, why the plate stayed hidden behind the radio rather than on the shelf with his tailoring prizes. __He pinned the hem, unpinned it, and pinned it again in exactly the same place.__ Then he said my name, Kagiso, as if starting over, and spoke of other things: the price of wool, my father's cough that winter, how quiet our house had been while my father lay in the hospital. A girl, he said, should have one thing to be proud of that has nothing to do with sickrooms. He did not mention chess. I looked at the plate a long time, and then at his hands, which never misjudged a move on cloth. Below, a bus ground its gears at the corner of Moi Avenue.
items.question: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
options: It shows Jomo's precision as a tailor, contrasting it with his lack of skill at chess.
It suggests Jomo is irritated by the question and wishes the narrator would stop asking.
It shows Jomo so absorbed in his work that he fails to hear the narrator's question.
It conveys Jomo's hesitation, hinting that the question touches something long concealed.

items.passage: Ma'am, this was in the type case, said the boy who brings the paper stock, holding out my husband's brass composing stick, which I had hunted for since the funeral. I thanked him coldly and counted the sorts in the drawer after he left. Widows in the press rooms of Port of Spain learn quickly that condolence and pilfering often arrive in the same hands. Yet he came back the next day to ask whether the stick had been set to the width of the Gazette or the hymn sheets, since the measure seemed odd to him. Only my husband had ever noticed such a thing. I showed him. He set three crooked lines, found each error himself, and reset them without a word of excuse. My sister-in-law Pearl tells everyone that Hortense has adopted a stray, and I let her. These days the composing stick is never where I leave it, and I have stopped counting the drawer. On the windowsill, the morning's proofs dry beside a jar of his marbles.
items.question: Which choice best describes the narrator's attitude toward the delivery boy?
options: Early suspicion that gradually softens into trust and quiet affection
Persistent wariness hidden beneath a show of polite gratitude
Pity for the boy's inexperience mixed with impatience at his errors
Grief-driven indifference that Pearl's teasing slowly breaks through

items.passage: Nova climbed the mountain road above Marrakesh with an envelope of cash sewn into a coat lining, and the storm shut both of them inside Dalia's cabin for three days. For a decade Nova had rehearsed this visit on night buses, polishing apologies until they shone. On the first morning Nova laid the envelope on the table; Dalia moved it aside to make room for the bread. On the second, they dug out the woodpile, and the shovel struck a tin box Dalia had buried long before. Inside lay the old receipts, each one crossed through in pencil gone gray with years. Dalia set the box by the stove and asked whether Nova still drew in the evenings. Beyond the window, wet snow slid from the cedar boughs and struck the drifts with a sound like breath let out.
items.question: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
options: To contrast Nova's long dread over the debt with Dalia's quiet, earlier release of it.
To recount how a snowstorm kept Nova in Dalia's cabin and led to a discovery.
To show how Dalia's buried records revealed the true amount Nova still owed her.
To suggest that old debts between relatives are best forgiven rather than repaid.

items.passage: Thandiwe had kept the boarding house on Bree Street for twenty years, and Lindiwe had lodged in its back room for nearly as long, paying in coins or, when coins were scarce, in reed mats woven to a pattern her grandmother had carried down from the hills. Buyers at the Saturday market sometimes asked who else made them. Lindiwe would only shrug. Lately she had begun leaving mats half finished on the windowsill, and in the mornings she ran her knuckles under the hot tap before she could close her hand around a cup. One winter evening Thandiwe cleared the kitchen table, laid out a bundle of reeds, and sat down with her sleeves rolled. Teach me, she said, before the pattern goes to sleep in your hands. Lindiwe snorted, but she pulled up a chair, and by the light of the stove the first rows appeared, crooked and stubborn. A kettle muttered on the back burner, and upstairs a lodger was practicing scales on a borrowed concertina.
items.question: As used in the text, the phrase “before the pattern goes to sleep in your hands” most nearly suggests
options: a hope that Lindiwe will finally rest after her many years of weaving.
the danger that the craft will vanish as Lindiwe's hands lose their strength.
the way the pattern has become so familiar that Lindiwe weaves without thought.
a worry that Lindiwe will keep the pattern secret from everyone in the house.

items.passage: Anniversaries matter to me. Ten years after my first novel appeared, I wanted a dinner on the harbor, speeches, a printed card with both our names. Eulalio, who had carried my sentences into English through three books, wanted nothing. We argued on the stairwell of my lodging on the Cornish coast, I on the landing, he two steps below, the skylight rattling in the sea wind. I reminded him that reviewers had praised the music of the English pages, and that he had asked for his name to be printed small on the title page, then smaller. He said that was rather the point. His part, he told me, had always been a lamp in the next room: enough to read by, never meant to be looked at. I wanted to argue that lamps can be thanked. Instead I asked him to write the card himself, in whatever size he liked. Overhead, a gull walked the slate roof, its claws scraping at every step.
items.question: As used in the text, the phrase “a lamp in the next room” most nearly suggests
options: a role that lets others see clearly while it remains out of sight itself.
a steady companionship that keeps Pilar from feeling alone as she writes.
a modest talent Eulalio hides because he doubts the quality of his work.
a sense of exclusion from the celebration Pilar has planned for the book.
